opus-5.5.text:
Benchmarks have played a really important role, but I think it's a double-edged sword.

On the positive side, a good benchmark gives the whole community a shared target. ImageNet is the classic example: once everyone could measure progress on the same dataset, you saw this rapid iteration, from AlexNet to ResNet and beyond. A benchmark turns a vague question like "is this model smart?" into something concrete and comparable, and that clarity accelerates research tremendously.

The problem is what happens once a benchmark becomes the target. Goodhart's law kicks in. People start optimizing for the benchmark itself rather than the underlying capability it was meant to measure. With large language models this has become quite serious. The training data is so huge, scraped from the whole internet, that test sets can leak into it, sometimes without anyone intending it. Then you see a high score and you don't really know whether the model is reasoning or just remembering. Benchmarks also saturate very quickly now. Something designed to be hard for years gets solved in months, and then it no longer tells you much.

So I think the role of benchmarks is shifting. Static benchmarks, a fixed set of questions with fixed answers, are less informative than before. What we need are things that are harder to game: dynamically generated problems, tasks where you can verify the answer but can't memorize it, like new math problems, coding tasks, or planning problems with combinatorial structure. That's part of why I've worked on reasoning and planning. In those settings you can construct fresh instances endlessly and actually test whether the model has learned the procedure rather than the pattern.

There's also a deeper point. Benchmarks measure what we already know how to measure. But some of the most important capabilities, like discovering something genuinely new, doing long-horizon research, or adapting to a novel situation, are very hard to put into a benchmark. If we only optimize for what's measurable, we might push models in a direction that looks great on paper but misses what really matters.

So my view is: benchmarks are necessary, they're the compass for the field, but we have to keep redesigning the compass. And as researchers we should keep asking whether the number going up actually means the model got better at the thing we care about.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks give the community a shared target, make progress comparable, and accelerate research, framing benchmark progress as a way to improve AI capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks make a vague question concrete and comparable, but does not describe breaking broad AI capability goals into smaller tasks with quantitative measures.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think benchmarks play a double role, and you have to hold both in your head at once.

On one hand, they are indispensable. Research is a community effort, and a benchmark is basically a shared language. It lets a thousand groups work on the same problem, compare results honestly, and know whether an idea actually works or just sounds good. A lot of the progress we've seen in deep learning came from exactly this: ImageNet, then the language modeling benchmarks, then math and coding datasets. Without a measurable target, you can't do systematic engineering, and you can't tell signal from noise.

On the other hand, every benchmark is a proxy, and the moment it becomes the target, it stops being a good proxy. Models get trained, directly or indirectly, toward the test. Data contamination creeps in. People overfit the evaluation format rather than the underlying skill. So a benchmark that was meaningful two years ago can be saturated today and tell you almost nothing. We've seen this many times; GSM8K was a real challenge once, and now it's basically a sanity check.

So my view is that benchmarks are a tool for the climb, not the summit. What I care about is whether the model has a general capability, and benchmarks are snapshots of that capability from particular angles. The healthy loop is: design a benchmark that captures something we can't do yet, work hard until it's solved, then be honest that it's solved and move to the next, harder one. The danger is when the community gets stuck optimizing a number after the number has lost its meaning.

I'd also add that the most interesting direction now is benchmarks that are hard to game. Things with verifiable answers, like math and code, where you can check correctness automatically. Open-ended tasks where the model has to plan over many steps, interact with an environment, and recover from mistakes. Those are much closer to what we actually want from these systems, and they generate training signal too, not just evaluation. In that sense, a good benchmark and a good training environment are becoming the same object.

r001.rationale: It presents benchmarks as measurable targets for making progress, says groups compare results and work until a benchmark is solved, and describes them as tools for developing general model capability.

r002.rationale: It calls benchmarks measurable targets and snapshots of capability from particular angles, but does not explain that they measure smaller tasks derived by breaking down broader AI capability goals.

astra-6.text:
I think benchmarks are very useful because they give researchers a common target. You have an idea, you run an experiment, and you can see whether it improves on previous methods. That makes progress much easier to measure and coordinate across the community.

But a benchmark is only a proxy for the capability we actually care about. If you optimize too much for a fixed test, the score can keep improving without the system becoming equally useful in real situations. It might exploit patterns in the dataset, or the evaluation might simply miss important weaknesses.

So I see benchmarks as part of a feedback loop. A good benchmark exposes something current models cannot do. Researchers make progress, and then we need to examine what the higher scores actually mean. Once the benchmark stops distinguishing meaningful improvements, we need harder or more realistic evaluations. The goal is to improve the underlying capability, and the benchmark helps us see whether we’re moving in that direction.

r001.rationale: It says benchmarks help measure and coordinate progress toward the underlying capability, framing scores as a means to capability improvement.

r002.rationale: It describes benchmarks as tests or proxies for capabilities, but does not say they quantify smaller tasks derived by breaking down broad AI goals.

sol-6.1.text:
I think benchmarks are very important because they give researchers a concrete target. You have an idea, you train a model, and you need some way to tell whether it actually improves things. A shared benchmark also allows different groups to compare results and build on each other’s work.

But a benchmark is always a proxy for the capability we really care about. If you optimize too much for a fixed test, you may improve the score without improving the underlying ability very much. And once a benchmark becomes saturated, it stops telling you where the interesting problems are.

So I see a cycle: we develop a benchmark, make progress on it, examine what the models still cannot do, and then develop better evaluations. For reasoning, for example, I would want to know whether a model can handle new variations of a problem, whether it can recover from a mistake, and whether its solution works—not just whether it produces the expected final answer. The benchmark should help us discover weaknesses as well as measure progress.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks provide targets and let groups compare progress, but it does not frame climbing benchmark leaderboards as a means to improve AI capabilities.

r002.rationale: It discusses benchmark scores and specific evaluation examples, but does not describe benchmarks as quantitative measures for smaller tasks derived by breaking down broad AI capability goals.
